summary.title: Reckon you've seen some stupid security things? Here, hold my beer...
summary.one_liner: A catalogue of real-world bad security practices from named companies, showing what not to do with passwords, cookies, resets, security questions and account enumeration.
takeaways: Storing a Base64-encoded password in a cookie is not protection; it is readable and must never be used for a remember-me feature.
Cookies holding sensitive data should be flagged Secure and HttpOnly, and reflected XSS must be fixed.
Password reset flows that rely on guessable data such as username and date of birth allow account takeover.
Account lookup endpoints that reveal whether an email exists, or return personal data for it, enable enumeration and data leaks.
Security questions based on immutable or guessable facts are weak and should be avoided.
summary.summary: Troy Hunt collects examples of poor security decisions from real companies, each tied to a tweet or a screenshot. Examples include a remember-me feature that stores a Base64-encoded password in an insecure cookie, a password reset that needed only a username and date of birth, weak security questions, and a checkout that disclosed personal data for any email address. The post is informal and opinionated rather than a step-by-step guide. Its value lies in the concrete anti-patterns it describes and why each is dangerous.
